demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
There is a moment that plays in her mind over and over, always the same. She is on the night shift at the warehouse, alone except for the hum of the security cameras. A man she does not recognize is walking through the loading bay. She calls out. He turns and runs. She follows-not to chase, only to identify-but he wheels around, fist raised. Instinct takes over. Her baton swings. The crack of it against his temple is a sound she hears in her sleep. He falls backward, his head hitting the concrete floor like a dropped melon. The blood pools before she even radios for help.

She is sixty-one now, a Pacific Islander woman who moved to this city twenty years ago for work. She has always been steady, a quiet presence in her uniform, the kind of guard who checks the gates twice and greets the late-shift workers by name. But that night changed her. The man survived, but he did not wake up for six weeks, and when he did, half his body did not move. She knows the details from the hospital report she cannot stop reading. She knows his wife's name, his children's ages. She knows she is the reason his son will never play soccer again.

At work, she avoids the loading bay. She requests only desk duty, sitting in front of a bank of monitors with her hands folded. When a co-worker pats her shoulder to say hello, she flinches. The sound of a dropped clipboard makes her heart race. She has started to doubt every decision. Last week, she let a delivery driver enter without checking his ID because she was afraid of being too aggressive, and her supervisor wrote her up. She lies awake after midnight shifts, replaying the second before she swung her baton, wondering if she could have simply stepped aside. She cannot remember the man's face, only the feel of the baton connecting.

She has stopped going to her church. The hymns remind her of forgiveness, and she cannot accept it. Her friends call, but she lets the phone ring. She tells herself they are better off without her. Twice she has driven to the hospital where the man is still in rehab, but each time she parks and then drives away, shaking. At home she drinks two glasses of rum every night to quiet the replaying loop.

Her PCL-5 score is seventy-six, but she does not know that number. All she knows is that every morning she wakes up and for one second she is the person she used to be-then the memory lands, heavy and cold, and she remembers what she did. She carries her guilt like a second uniform. It never comes off.
